title: How Capital Gains Taxes Work When You Sell a Home
bigPicture: When you sell your home for more than you paid, the profit is usually tax-free up to $250,000 (single) or $500,000 (married), if you lived there 2 of the last 5 years.
whatYouNeedToKnow: Capital gains tax is just a tax on the profit you make, not the whole sale price.
The IRS lets most homeowners skip tax on up to $250,000 of profit ($500,000 if married filing jointly).
You must have lived in the home as your main home for at least 2 years out of the last 5 to qualify.
Money you spent on big improvements (new roof, kitchen remodel) adds to your cost basis and lowers your taxable profit.
Even if you owe no tax, you still must report the sale on your return.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Forgetting to save receipts for home improvements — they lower your tax.
Assuming every sale is tax-free — the 2-of-5-year rule must be met.
Not reporting the sale because you think you owe nothing.
Selling a second home and expecting the same big exclusion — it only applies to your main home.
actionSteps: Gather all receipts for upgrades and repairs done in the last few years.
Write down what you paid for the home plus improvement costs — that's your cost basis.
Subtract cost basis from the sale price to find your profit.
Check if you meet the 2-of-5-year live-in rule.
Talk to a tax preparer or use IRS Form 8949 to report the sale correctly.
